Hansa had practised her Annual Day speech on water conservation for two weeks: a story to open, three points, a question to close. She was on third. Then, as she reached the podium, the microphone died with a squeal. Four hundred students and parents stirred and started chatting.
Her hands went cold. Her friend Jomon, running the sound desk, mouthed, "Two minutes!"
Hansa didn't wait. She stepped to the front edge of the stage, planted her feet like her drama teacher taught, and said loudly, "Raise your hand if your tap ran dry this summer."
Hands shot up. The chatter stopped.
She spoke slower than in practice, looking at the back row, pausing after each point. When the mic crackled back on halfway through, she waved it away.
Afterwards, Jomon handed her a bottle of water. "You didn't even need me."

qa.q: How many students and parents were in the audience?
qa.a: Four hundred students and parents.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when the microphone died?
qa.a: Hansa felt nervous, her hands going cold, but she chose to act instead of freezing.

qa.q: What choice kept the audience with Hansa, and why?
qa.a: Asking a question that everyone could answer with a raised hand, because it pulled attention back to her without needing the microphone.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel watching from the sound desk?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt stressed about the broken mic at first, then relieved and proud when Hansa held the audience on her own.

grounding: Shows a teenager using a clear structure and calm stage habits to hold an audience when the microphone fails.

Sachin, put the phone down for one minute. I want to tell you something that happened to me when I was thirty.
I'd started watching cooking videos at night. Harmless, no? But slowly the app began showing me angry ones: people shouting about food prices, then about neighbours, then about everyone. I'd watch one, and it gave me ten more. I'd look up and it was two in the morning, and I was furious about strangers.
Your Phuphi Zeenat, a sensible woman, got angry at the whole world for no reason.
One day your uncle asked, "Did you choose any of this?" I hadn't. The app chose, because anger kept me watching.
So I did three things: turned off autoplay, stopped liking the angry clips, and put the phone in the kitchen at ten. Took a month to feel normal.
Now, what does your feed show you most?

qa.q: What time did Phuphi Zeenat move the phone to the kitchen?
qa.a: Zeenat put the phone in the kitchen at ten.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling during those late nights of watching?
qa.a: Zeenat felt angry and restless, furious about strangers without really knowing why.

qa.q: Which step inside Zeenat's story made the turning point?
qa.a: The uncle's question, "Did you choose any of this?", made Zeenat see the app was choosing for her, which led her to change her settings and habits.

qa.q: How might Sachin's uncle have seen the change in Zeenat?
qa.a: The uncle likely felt worried to see Zeenat angry at the world, and relieved when she noticed it and took steps to change.

grounding: Shows an elder explaining to a teenager how a feed learned to keep Zeenat watching and how Zeenat took control back.

passage:
I'm Uday, Ishita's older brother. Last month I noticed she'd stopped eating properly and jumped every time her phone buzzed.
One night she came to my room, shaking, and showed me her messages. Someone she'd met in a game, who said he was sixteen, had got a photo of her face and made it into a fake picture. Now he was saying, "Send more or I share this with your school. Don't tell anyone."
I told her, "This isn't your fault. You did right by showing me." We woke Mummy and Papa right then. Papa took screenshots, and they reported the account on the cybercrime portal that night. Next morning they went to the police station and told her class teacher, just in case.
She blocked him and hasn't replied since. I don't know everything she felt, but she slept in Mummy's room for a week, and slowly started laughing again.

qa.q: What did the person threaten to do?
qa.a: He said he would share the fake picture with her school.

qa.q: What was Ishita likely feeling before she showed Uday the messages?
qa.a: She was likely terrified and ashamed, jumping every time her phone buzzed and not eating properly.

qa.q: Which choice protected Ishita best, and why?
qa.a: Telling her brother, who woke their parents that same night to save evidence and report it, because trusted adults could stop the blackmail and she didn't face it alone.

qa.q: How does Uday respond to seeing his sister in this situation?
qa.a: Uday stays calm and protective, telling her it isn't her fault and bringing in their parents straight away.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising online blackmail, ending contact and getting trusted adults to report it the same night.

In the hostel study hall, Gautam, sixteen, dozed off with his head on his chemistry book. Warden Sarita Ma'am tapped the desk. "Third time this week."
"Sorry, ma'am. Couldn't sleep."
She sat down beside him. "Couldn't, or didn't?"
Gautam thought about the night before: one reel, then another, then a gaming match that ended at 2:40. He'd told himself "five more minutes" at least six times.
"Didn't," he admitted. "I don't even enjoy it after midnight. I just can't stop."
Sarita Ma'am nodded. "What would help you stop?"
He thought. "If the phone's not near the bed. And if I stop the game at eleven, even mid-match."
That night he left his phone charging at the warden's desk. His roommate Aarav laughed at him. By Friday, Aarav's phone was charging there too.

qa.q: What time did Gautam's gaming match end the night before?
qa.a: It ended at 2:40.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he admitted "I just can't stop"?
qa.a: Gautam felt frustrated and a bit ashamed, knowing the late-night scrolling no longer felt good but struggling to stop.

qa.q: What did Sarita Ma'am do well in this conversation?
qa.a: She asked questions instead of scolding, so Gautam named the problem himself and chose his own limits.

qa.q: Why might Aarav go from laughing to charging his phone there too?
qa.a: Aarav may have noticed Gautam sleeping better and realised he had the same problem, so the joke turned into a shared habit.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing compulsive late-night phone use and setting his own limits.

Dear Anjali Didi,
You're the only one I can tell this to without being teased.
For months I've been watching gym videos every night. Guys my age with huge arms, perfect abs. I started skipping Ammi's rotis and doing push-ups till my wrists hurt. Last week a boy at the gym offered me a powder "to grow fast" and said not to tell my parents.
I didn't buy it. But I wanted to.
Then I remembered what you said when you were sixteen and stopped eating lunch: "Those photos aren't real life." You looked so tired that year.
So I'm going to talk to Coach about a proper training plan and ask Ammi to take me to the doctor before I try anything. And I'm eating the rotis again.
I still don't like my arms. But maybe I can like them a bit more later.
Wasim

qa.a: The boy offered a powder "to grow fast".

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when the boy offered the powder?
qa.a: Wasim felt tempted and insecure about body image, even though something about it felt wrong.

qa.q: What wise steps is Wasim taking now?
qa.a: Wasim is talking to Coach about a proper plan, asking Ammi for a doctor visit before trying anything, and eating meals again.

qa.q: How might Anjali Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Anjali would probably feel touched that her old words helped, and relieved that Wasim reached out before trying the powder.

grounding: Shows a teenager struggling with idealised body images but choosing safe, supported habits over harmful ones.

In the Class 9 science lab, Farida's test tube cracked. Pradeep, her lab partner, said, "Careful, you'll break everything."
"Maybe if you did something instead of watching!" Farida snapped, loud enough for the whole row to hear.
Pradeep went quiet. Farida's face burned. She didn't know why she was so angry. Yesterday she'd cried at a movie and this morning she'd shouted at her little brother over a sock.
At break, she sat on the stairs alone. The biology teacher passing by stopped. "Rough day?"
"I keep getting angry for nothing, Ma'am."
"Moods can swing a lot at your age. That's normal. But you still get to choose what you do next."
After break, Farida found Pradeep at the tap. "Sorry. That was about me, not you."
Pradeep shrugged, then smiled. "I was watching too much, though."

qa.q: What happened to Farida's test tube?
qa.a: Farida's test tube cracked.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling after snapping at Pradeep?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed and confused, her face burning, not understanding why she was so angry.

qa.q: What did the teacher's words help Farida do?
qa.a: They helped her see that moods can swing at her age but she can still choose her actions, so she went and apologised.

qa.q: How does Pradeep respond to Farida's apology?
qa.a: Pradeep accepts it easily, even admitting his own part, which shows he wasn't holding a grudge.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing sudden mood swings and choosing to apologise instead of letting the mood decide.

The concert was on Saturday night, ending at eleven, and my parents' curfew was nine. Last year I'd have slammed my door. I'm Manoj, seventeen, and this time I tried something else.
I waited till after dinner, when Papa was relaxed. I said, "I know you worry. Here's the plan." I showed them: who was going, how we'd get there and back, that Trisha's father would drop us home by 11:30. I offered to text every hour.
Papa said, "Eleven-thirty is too late." My face got hot. I wanted to argue. Instead I asked, "What time would feel okay?"
We settled on midnight at the gate, with the texts. Ma added one rule: if anything felt wrong, I call and they come, no questions.
I texted every hour. I was home at 11:40. Next time, Papa said, I can ask directly.

qa.q: Who would drop them home by 11:30?
qa.a: Trisha's father would drop them home.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Papa said eleven-thirty was too late?
qa.a: Manoj felt frustrated and defensive, face getting hot, but chose to stay calm.

qa.q: Which part of Manoj's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking "What time would feel okay?" instead of arguing, because it made the curfew a shared decision and built trust.

qa.q: How do Manoj's parents see the result?
qa.a: They seem reassured and more trusting, since Papa says Manoj can ask directly next time.

grounding: Shows a teenager respectfully negotiating more freedom and a later curfew with parents.

I'm Pankaj, and I sit behind Jahnavi in Class 11. When the mock test ranks came out, she dropped from third to nineteenth. She stared at the list, then folded it very small and put it in her pocket.
At lunch she didn't eat. She said, "Papa will ask who came first. He always does."
A week later, she wasn't laughing in class anymore. I told our class teacher I was worried about her. The teacher called her in that afternoon and asked the school counsellor to join. I don't know what they talked about.
But the next Monday, Jahnavi said, "The counsellor asked me what I actually got wrong. It was mostly one chapter." She'd made a plan for it. She also said her mother came to meet the counsellor too.
She's still nervous before tests. But she's eating lunch again.

qa.q: What rank did Jahnavi drop to?
qa.a: She dropped from third to nineteenth.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi folding the list very small suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt ashamed and anxious, wanting to hide her rank and dreading her father's question.

qa.q: What small step helped Jahnavi cope with the rank?
qa.a: Looking with the counsellor at what she actually got wrong showed it was mostly one chapter, so she could make a plan instead of feeling like a failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Pankaj to watch Jahnavi change?
qa.a: Pankaj was worried enough to tell the class teacher, and now seems relieved to see her eating lunch again.

grounding: Shows a teenager coping with rank pressure and parental expectations with support from a teacher and counsellor.
